title: Japan September services PPI holds at 3.7% y/y, in line with forecast, before BoJ
body: An in-line print is unlikely to move the yen much on its own, but it removes one possible dovish surprise before Friday's decision and keeps the backdrop supportive of December hike pricing. Steady services inflation strengthens the case for the Outlook Report to effectively declare underlying inflation has reached 2%, which would support the yen and short-end JGB yields. The bigger moves are still likely to come from the BoJ's vote split, Ueda's press conference and Wednesday's Fed decision. Oil-driven cost pressure tied to the Iran conflict keeps the wider inflation backdrop firm. --- Earlier: BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk Japan services PPI preview: 3.7% pace in focus ahead of Friday's BoJ decision --- Japan's firms are still passing on service costs at a two-year-high pace, handing the BoJ one more piece of evidence for the 2% declaration markets expect this week.

title: Greer warns $3.4 billion EU loan to Airbus may breach US-EU aircraft trade truce Alt headlines:
body: This is a warning shot rather than an escalation, so the immediate market impact is likely confined to aerospace names, with Airbus and Boeing shares the most exposed to any shift in trade rhetoric. The bigger risk is that aircraft financing becomes a fresh front in US-EU trade tensions at a time when the administration is already fighting on several fronts, including Canada. Any move toward formal measures, such as reviving tariffs linked to the old subsidy dispute, would weigh on European aerospace and the wider supply chain. A quick EU response with loan details would likely defuse the issue. --- The Boeing-Airbus feud is back on Washington's radar, with Greer warning that Europe's record loan to Airbus could unpick a hard-won aircraft truce unless Brussels starts sharing details.

title: Australia CPI preview: banks see 1.0% core rise, above the RBA's 0.8% forecast
body: The Australian dollar and front-end yields are set up for a binary reaction. With implied hike odds already above half, a trimmed mean at or above 1.0% would push November pricing closer to fully priced and support the currency. A 0.9% or lower print could see that pricing unwind quickly. Oil is central to the headline story: the fuel spike reflects the global energy shock tied to the Iran conflict, so further gains in crude would keep headline inflation elevated into year-end. The services component matters most for the RBA, since broadening price pressure would undercut the argument that this is purely an imported energy shock. The release coincides with RBA officials appearing before Senate Estimates, adding to the event risk. --- Earlier: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac's Ellis says read the data calls --- Australia's core inflation is set to overshoot the RBA's own forecast for another quarter, and with the banks split down the middle, Wednesday's print may decide whether the Board hikes on Melbourne Cup Day.

title: RBA is talking more but promising nothing: Westpac's Ellis says read the data calls
body: For rates traders, the note argues against reading too much into tone shifts between the press conference and market-focused speeches, and in favour of the minutes and officials' data interpretations as the cleaner signal. The Governor describing the labour market as a little tight, plus staff's downbeat view of supply capacity, leans hawkish and supports pricing for further tightening rather than a pause. The coming fortnight is dense with event risk for the Australian dollar and front-end yields: the quarterly CPI lands alongside Senate Estimates testimony, followed by the November decision, the Statement on Monetary Policy and further speeches. With supply shocks driving inflation, including energy, a firm CPI would reinforce the hawkish read. --- Yesterday: RBA's Hunter says inflation job not done after four hikes, November rise in view --- The RBA has never been chattier, but Westpac's Luci Ellis says traders hunting for promises should listen instead to how it reads the data, because that is where the real signal lives.

title: ROADMAP: Morgan Stanley sees three catalysts ending the correction to ~7150, then S&P 500 to 8,000
body: Morgan Stanley's Wilson's framework gives traders a roadmap: a final flush toward 7,100 to 7,200, slightly below the 200-day moving average, would be consistent with his view rather than a breakdown of it. The quality factor breaking out suggests leadership stays defensive until his catalysts clear, while beaten-down early-cycle groups such as semiconductors carry the most rebound potential once they do. The liquidity call is the key one to watch: any signal from the Fed on slowing balance sheet growth further, or on tightening financial conditions, would matter more for his timeline than AI headlines. Oil-driven inflation that keeps the Fed on its hiking path is the main threat to a quick resolution. --- Earlier: Citadel Securities warns AI trade has little margin for error as three risks converge Goldman Sachs: AI buildout to add up to 50bp to US core PCE, but the boost is temporary --- Wilson says the worst of the correction has already happened beneath the surface, and once AI, the midterms and Fed liquidity clear, the index can catch up with an 8,000 year-end target.

title: BoJ preview: MUFG sees hold but a 2% inflation call, with two dissenters the key yen risk
body: A hold with an effective 2% declaration and a firm Ueda press conference would support the yen and pull December hike pricing forward, pushing short-end JGB yields higher. The asymmetric risk is the vote: if the two reflationist members switch from opposing a hike to calling for a cut, the dovish signal could outweigh the hawkish language and trigger yen selling. USD/JPY is also exposed to this week's Fed meeting. A surprise US hike that sent the pair sharply higher is the kind of emergency that, per the Nikkei report, could put a back-to-back BoJ move on the table. Oil-driven inflation pressure from the Iran conflict adds to the case for a firmer BoJ tone. --- Earlier: BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral Nikkei slips, bounces, as Iran oil fears weigh; ING sees BOJ holding at 1.25%, two hikes in 2027 Still to come: Japan services PPI preview: 3.7% pace in focus ahead of Friday's BoJ decision --- The BoJ is set to stand still on rates this week while moving a big step forward on rhetoric, unless two dovish dissenters steal the headlines and the yen pays for it.

title: ICYMI: Morgan Stanley sees 10%-15% more downside for Chinese offshore stocks before a bottom
body: The call sets a clear valuation marker: offshore Chinese shares near eight times forward earnings would be historically cheap territory, and that could become a reference point for bottom-fishing. Until then, Hong Kong-listed Chinese stocks look more exposed than mainland shares, which Morgan Stanley sees as cushioned by government support. The link to the global AI sell-off means Chinese equities are trading partly as a proxy for global risk appetite. Further weakness in US tech could spill over even without fresh domestic news. Any sign of policy support or clarity on the trust tax issue would be the obvious upside risk to the bearish view. --- Yesterday: Goldman Sachs cuts Kospi target 25% to 9,000, still sees over 60% upside --- Morgan Stanley thinks China's stock slide has another leg to go before valuations hit their historical floor, though it still sees Beijing's support making mainland shares the safer place to wait.

title: FX option expiries for 27 October 10am New York cut
body: There are a couple of key expiry levels to take note of on the day, as highlighted in bold below. The first is for EUR/USD at the 1.1175 level, with the strike holding roughly within 10 pips of the spot price. That could help keep price action more contained around current levels, particularly with markets awaiting major central bank decisions later this week. Having said that, the technical downside momentum looks to be taking over again for EUR/USD and that could open up a push towards testing the month's lows around 1.1111 in the bigger picture. Then, there is a sizable cluster of expiries for USD/JPY layered between 157.75 to 158.00. All three are sitting just above the current spot price, so they could exert some magnetic pull on price action and potentially keep the pair more anchored around the region ahead of the cut later. However, just be wary that any fresh intervention warnings from Japanese officials could easily override that influence. And lastly, there is one for AUD/USD at the 0.7030 level - just a little over 10 pips away from the spot price. That could also act as a potential magnet for price action, with the expiry level tying closely with the 100-day moving average at 0.7031 currently. Put together, that could act as a bit of a resistance point for AUD/USD in the session ahead should trading conditions remain relatively subdued.

title: Japan finance minister Katayama warns of decisive action as yen intervention risks linger
body: Japan finance minister Katayama is out with another warning to markets today, reaffirming that Tokyo remains ready to step in if necessary to defend the yen. Her comments: Government stands ready to take decisive action in the FX market Always watching market moves with a high sense of urgency, including at this very moment Must ensure yen movements reflect economic fundamentals Hopes to maintain market trust in the yen and the Takaichi administration's fiscal policy through transparent, consistent communication Her remarks are not anything that we haven't heard of before. But as always, it is best for traders to take note on the tone and frequency of the communication. The comments above certainly underscore a more firm language, particularly the reference to taking "decisive action". Then again, it is a phrase that Tokyo officials have used in the past in associating with the threat of direct currency intervention. Having said that, I wouldn't read too much into the remarks as suggesting that intervention is imminent. As mentioned above, Katayama has used similarly forceful language before. So if anything else, this feels like Tokyo attempting to keep the pressure on yen sellers rather than signalling an immediate move. For now, USD/JPY is seeing a modest rebound after the sharp drop on Thursday last week. The pair is trading back above the 157 mark and is starting to take another look at key resistance in the form of the 200-day moving average at around 158.51.

title: Bond market tensions ease but Treasury yields near 5% and France's debt risks keep investors on edge
body: There is a bit of a welcome relief in global bonds to start the new week, particularly in Europe after Moody's affirmed France's Aa3 credit rating. Meanwhile, Treasury yields have also settled down a fair bit after an extremely volatile period earlier this month. But in looking at where things are right now, there is still plenty of tension lurking beneath the surface. For one, 10-year Treasury yields are still sitting just below the 5% mark for the time being. And over in Europe, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread remains at levels that would have surely been alarming just a few months ago. So while the selling pressure in the bond market has eased for now, the underlying concerns haven't really changed all that much. And as much as that offers some breathing room for broader markets, there are still plenty of reasons to be cautious. The Fed decision tomorrow is one obvious catalyst, even if policymakers are widely expected to leave interst rates unchanged. And beyond that, I'm also keeping a close watch on big tech earnings this week. On the latter, there's a growing concern over whether the enormous spending behind the AI boom can actually justify the returns. And if earnings from the likes of Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon all back that sentiment, we could see a rather nasty bout of volatility kick in again. That will especially be the case if investors start seeking safety in government bonds again while becoming more wary of riskier corporate debt.

title: European markets face a quiet calendar today as central banks and big tech earnings loom
body: European traders will be greeted with a rather bare economic calendar when they get to their desks today, and I reckon that might suit some market players just fine considering what is on the agenda later this week. In terms of data releases, we only have French consumer confidence for October and the ECB's survey on euro area lending for September. Otherwise, markets will largely be left to their own devices as traders wait on the central bank bonanza to roll into town. Wall Street at least provided a more positive lead in overnight trading, with the S&P 500 posting 0.7% gains and the Nasdaq closing 0.8% higher. Tech stocks helped to drive the rebound but caution is very much still up in the air, especially with the recent volatility surrounding the AI trade. As for geopolitical tensions, we are seeing more of the same old, same old. Fresh diplomatic efforts involving Iran are offering some hope of de-escalation but continued attacks on Saudi Arabia are keeping oil supply risks firmly in the picture. As such, I wouldn't be surprised if we see traders take on a more reserved and cautious approach to trading today. After all, the focus now turns to the BOC and Fed decisions tomorrow, followed by the ECB on Thursday and BOJ on Friday. And that is without mentioning big tech earnings with Microsoft, Alphabet, and Amazon all set to put the AI spending debate back under the spotlight.

title: Ethereum Foundation "dump" is a $6.4m treasury sale, not a crisis
body: A sale of this size has no meaningful effect on ETH supply or price, coming in at well under 0.1% of daily trading volume. The more relevant support for ETH is around $2,300, where it has been trading, and the broader flow picture: buying from Bitmine is fading, and spot ETF flows matter more than one-off Foundation conversions. A series of larger Foundation sales into weakness would be the scenario that turns this into a genuine supply story. --- Crypto Twitter called it a dump, but the Ethereum Foundation selling $6.4 million of ETH to cover its running costs is a budget line, not a bear signal. Summary: The Ethereum Foundation sold around 2,785 ETH, worth about $6.4 million, for the USDS stablecoin on CoW Swap Social media posts framed the sale as the Foundation dumping ETH The sale equals well under 0.1% of a single day's ETH trading volume, and less than Bitmine bought last week The Foundation's treasury policy sets out regular ETH sales to fund operations when cash reserves fall below about 2.5 years of costs It cut its 2026 budget by around 40% and stakes about 70,000 ETH to reduce reliance on sales The Ethereum Foundation sold around 2,785 ETH, worth roughly $6.4 million, according to on-chain tracker Onchain Lens, swapping the tokens for USDS, the dollar stablecoin issued by the Sky ecosystem, through the decentralised exchange CoW Swap. Within minutes, crypto Twitter had turned a routine treasury transaction into the Foundation "dumping" ETH.

It does sharpen focus on the tension in this week's Fed decision. With 10-year yields near 5% and credit spreads wider, any hawkish surprise from the Fed risks further pressure on rate-sensitive sectors such as housing and leveraged borrowers. title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6731 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.
